title: Measuring Success

character.name: The Scorekeeper
character.tagline: Pick the wrong metric and you'll celebrate the wrong victory.

oneLiner: The metrics that tell you if a model is actually good — precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, and friends.
analogy: Imagine a fishing net. Precision asks: 'Of everything I caught, how much was actually fish (not boots)?' Recall asks: 'Of all the fish in the sea, how many did I catch?' A huge net catches every fish (high recall) but also tons of junk (low precision). A tiny net catches only obvious fish (high precision) but misses many (low recall). F1 is the referee that balances the two. The Scorekeeper's rule: choose the metric that matches what costs you — missing cancer (recall) vs annoying healthy patients (precision).
objectives: Understand precision, recall, and F1 and when each matters.
Read a confusion matrix (true/false positives and negatives).
Interpret ROC-AUC for classifiers and RMSE/MAE for regression.
Pick metrics aligned to the real-world cost of errors.
keyConcepts: A confusion matrix breaks predictions into true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives.
Precision = of predicted positives, how many were correct (avoids false alarms).
Recall = of actual positives, how many were found (avoids misses).
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall — useful when you need balance, especially on imbalanced data.
ROC-AUC summarizes classifier performance across thresholds (1.0 = perfect, 0.5 = random).
For regression, RMSE and MAE measure average prediction error (RMSE punishes big misses more).
The 'best' metric depends on which error is costlier for your use case.

scenarios.scenario: A cancer-screening model must avoid missing sick patients, even if it means some false alarms that get double-checked later.
scenarios.question: Which metric should you prioritize?

options.label: Recall — catching as many true positives as possible

scenarios.explanation: Missing a sick patient (a false negative) is the costly error here, so you prioritize recall — even at the expense of some false positives that follow-up tests can catch.

quiz.question: Precision answers which question?
options: Of all actual positives, how many did we find?
Of everything we predicted positive, how many were actually positive?
How many layers does the model have?
quiz.answer: Of everything we predicted positive, how many were actually positive?
quiz.explanation: Precision = TP / (TP + FP): among predicted positives, the fraction that were correct. It penalizes false alarms.

quiz.question: Recall answers which question?
options: Of all actual positives, how many did the model correctly identify?
Of predicted positives, how many were right?
What is the model's memory usage?
quiz.answer: Of all actual positives, how many did the model correctly identify?
quiz.explanation: Recall = TP / (TP + FN): among real positives, the fraction the model caught. It penalizes misses.

quiz.question: The F1 score is:
options: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing the two
quiz.answer: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing the two
quiz.explanation: F1 combines precision and recall into one number, useful when you care about both and especially under class imbalance.

quiz.question: An ROC-AUC of 0.5 indicates a classifier that is:
quiz.explanation: AUC ranges 0.5 (random) to 1.0 (perfect ranking). 0.5 means the model can't distinguish positives from negatives.

quiz.question: For a regression model, which metric measures average prediction error and punishes large errors more?
quiz.explanation: RMSE squares errors before averaging, so big misses weigh more. MAE (mean absolute error) treats all errors linearly.
